Life, Death and Rebirth in the Land of the Buddha

The New York Times May 14, 2026

The Prince’s Journey

The Prince’s Journey

Starting at the birthplace of Buddhism, a writer traces how its teachings spread across Asia, transforming the continent forever.

The Prince’s Journey

Starting at the birthplace of Buddhism, a writer traces how its teachings spread across Asia, transforming the continent forever.

The view from Swayambhunath Stupa, built in the fifth century and a pilgrimage site for both Hindus and Buddhists, of Wochen Thukje Choeling Monastery in the Kathmandu Valley, in Nepal. Credit... Keerthana Kunnath

Supported by

By Aatish Taseer

Photographs by Keerthana Kunnath

This is the first chapter of Aatish Taseer’s three-part travel feature tracing the spread of Buddhism across Asia. Click here to read the second chapter, on Thailand, and here for the third chapter, on Taiwan.

ON A PALE October day, I found myself at the birthplace of the Buddha. A short flight on Buddha Air from Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu, had brought me south to Lumbini, where the Awakened One was born around 563 B. C. There, in the shade of a peepul tree, I sat down with Basanta Kumar Bidari, a retired archaeologist. I was acutely aware that it was under such a tree, some 25 centuries before, that the Buddha had acquired the knowledge that set him free from the cycle of death and rebirth.

The Buddha had spent the entire duration of his 80-year life in this region that lay between Nepal and northeastern India, just across the border from Lumbini. Two centuries after his death, an Indian emperor, Ashoka the Great, who ruled over the majority of modern India, erected a pillar at the place of his birth. Legend has it that Ashoka converted to Buddhism after a battle of conquest filled him with remorse over the loss of human life. His conversion electrified the spread of the new doctrine, in much the same way that Constantine’s would do for Christianity six centuries later.

Bidari, who’d devoted three decades of his life to this site in Lumbini, wanted to draw my attention to three words in the inscription upon the Ashokan pillar that still had the power to make the 70-year-old archaeologist’s hair stand on end: “atana agācha mahīyte,” “I myself came here.” “There are so many Ashokan pillars and edicts,” he said, “but none have these words.” It was a testament to the significance of Lumbini. The site had been consecrated twice, first by the Buddha himself, then by Ashoka, whose emissaries had gone all over the civilized world promoting the new doctrine, and who wanted all to know that he’d come as a pilgrim to this spot.

Gazing out at the sunlit pillar — the white-walled Maya Devi Temple, with its gold finial, in the distance, beyond a tank of green water on whose steps turtles sunned themselves — I remembered first hearing the story of the Buddha’s awakening from my mother as a child in Delhi. Even then, I loved certain details: a 29-year-old prince named Siddhartha Gautama, seized by a horror of illness, old age and death, set out from his palace by cover of night. He was ready to abandon his young wife and child to find an answer to the problem of suffering. The gates of the palace, though guarded against his departure by his father, King Suddhodana, opened magically. Once the prince was far away, he removed his fineries and gave them to his charioteer. Then, after shaving his head, he began to live the life of a wandering ascetic in India, which was as easy for me to imagine in the 1980s as it would have been in the sixth century B. C. What was harder to understand was the almost Hamlet-like sensitivity of the Buddha — “I was delicate, extremely delicate, too delicate,” he would tell his disciples — and his tendency, as the Indian author Pankaj Mishra writes in “An End to Suffering: The Buddha in the World” (2004), “of noticing suffering as if no one had noticed it before.” I had grown up in India hardened to the horrors of poverty, and Siddhartha, before his awakening, struck me as too precious, too cosseted — a nepo baby if ever there was one!

In the three-part cover story for T’s Travel issue, Aatish Taseer follows Buddhism’s journey through Nepal, Thailand and Taiwan.

Plus: we share a map and timeline of the religion’s transmission across the East, a glossary of Buddhist terms, a snapshot of the great diversity of Buddhist monuments and an essential reading list. Click here to read Hanya Yanagihara’s editor’s letter.

The Buddha lived in a world where an older form of Hinduism, now known as Vedic, prevailed. (The Vedas are early Hindu texts dating from as far back as 1500 B. C.) It was a world of small tribal kingdoms giving way to political centralization and empire building. It was also a world full of monks, ascetics and teachers, and this is first and foremost what the Buddha was — a great Indian teacher, perhaps the greatest, but one of many in a tradition that continues to this day. The Indic religions, like most earth religions, with their deification of nature and their wide distribution of sanctity, do not deal in received wisdom. There are no prophets, no sons or messengers of God, no books that claim to be divine revelation. God, in the Abrahamic sense of the word, doesn’t really exist. “We are seekers, not believers,” a Nepali monk, Anil Sakya, 65, would say to me in Bangkok. The concept of “thou shalt not” was as alien to the Buddhist scheme, Sakya explained, as were mortal sins, lists of commandments, apocrypha and canons.

In a sermon called the Kalama Sutta, witnessed by Siddhartha’s cousin and attendant, Ananda — the man Sakya referred to as “the tape recorder” — the Buddha urges his followers to interrogate his teaching and to accept nothing blindly. “Ehipassiko,” he tells them, as later rendered in Pali, one of Buddhism’s liturgical languages, “come and see” (i. e., if the teaching is any good). Buddhism, with its nearly 330 million adherents stretching across more than a dozen countries, from Nepal to Japan, may outwardly seem like a religion in the Western sense, but that’s more an irony than a fact. “Siddhartha Gautama had sought to emancipate people from rituals and idolatry,” wrote the Hindi poet Harivansh Rai Bachchan in his 1958 narrative poem “Buddha and the Dance Hall,” yet “his devotees crafted elaborate rituals and made an idol of him. He preached against transactional worship; they converted him into an object of worship. He disbelieved in gods; they extolled him as God.”

In one respect, though, Buddhism did resemble other religions: It had places of pilgrimage, like Lumbini — the “sight of which should arouse a sense of urgency in the faithful,” Buddha is said to have told Ananda. (His sermons were conveyed orally for centuries.) For a thousand years or more, as Bidari told me, a steady stream of pilgrims, kings, monks and translators came in Ashoka’s wake to Lumbini. But then, around the 14th century, a number of factors, including Islamic invasions and a resurgent Hinduism, led to Buddhism leaving India for good, and all traffic to Lumbini ceased. “For 500 years,” Bidari said almost fearfully, “Lumbini went dark.”

It was an awesome thing to consider. Taking in the scene, where all around us the blackened remains of brick stupas pushed through the grass and red-bottomed rhesus monkeys prowled, I ransacked my mind for any historical analogue. It would be as if the whereabouts of Mecca or Bethlehem had been lost to Islam and Christianity and, even though the religions continued to flourish in the world beyond, no one knew where their founders had come from — that Muhammad was Arabian, or Christ a Jew. This was the situation when European rule took hold in India in the 18th century: Even the Indian origin of Siddhartha Gautama was lost to recorded history.

GROWING UP IN India, I was haunted by the absence left by the Buddha and his doctrine in his own homeland. It was why I’d undertaken this specific journey — to follow the doctrine east out of South Asia, into Southeast Asia and then finally to East Asia. I was fascinated not just by that absence but by the elasticity of Buddhism, the way that the dharma — a uniquely difficult word to translate, “dharma” can mean “duty,” “vocation,” “religion” but also “nature,” “essence,” “law” and “doctrine” — could bend and adapt to local culture, absorbing the Bon religion of the Tibetans or shamanism in Mongolia, while somehow also remaining true to itself. Over the years, I’d been to practically every major Buddhist country, save mainland China and Bhutan, and what stood out everywhere was the doctrine’s talent for localization. But for this trip, I’d restrict my itinerary to just three societies in order to look at three major strains of Buddhism: esoteric, or Vajrayana (the “Diamond” or “Thunderbolt Vehicle”) Buddhism in Nepal, which appeared around the fifth century A. D. and was rife with magic, secret rites, rituals and practices; Theravada (“the Way of the Elders”) in Thailand, which was nearly as old as Siddhartha himself and distinguished by monastic rules and scholasticism; and Mahayana (or “Great Vehicle”) in Taiwan, the strain that took hold in China around the sixth century and, later, all across northern Asia and Vietnam. There, away from the watchful gaze of the mainland’s Communist Party, I would be able to see how Buddhism had mixed with Taoism and Confucianism to produce the rich confection that is Chinese Buddhism.

The historic adaptability of the dharma was given fresh urgency by Buddhism’s ability to speak to our current moment. In an age when most religions had failed to provide good answers to the loss of old ways and the onslaught of materialism and technology, responding often as agents of fanaticism, nostalgia and backwardness, Buddhism (though not entirely exempt) had fared far better than the rest. Even anecdotally, it appeared in places where I couldn’t envision another creed flourishing. The writer George Saunders, a practicing Tibetan Buddhist, has spoken of how it allowed him to depersonalize his thoughts. The jazz pianist Herbie Hancock has followed a strain of Japanese Buddhism since the 1970s that emphasizes chanting “namu-myoho-renge-kyou” (“to devote oneself to the mystic law of the Lotus Sutra”) as a way to bring about inner transformation. At a hotel in upstate New York, awash in Scandinavian architecture and moneyed Brooklynites, a Tibetan master was offering “a blessing for peace and clarity” at a “sacred sound bath.” It was hard to imagine the same invitation being extended to a rabbi, a priest or an imam. Buddhism now spoke to global elites as few other traditions could, sometimes meaningfully, sometimes as pure woo-woo, and I was eager to know why.

AS BIDARI AND I stood in the hot morning sun at the entrance of what is now a sprawling complex of three square miles at Lumbini, the archaeologist credited two men for its existence. The first was Emperor Ashoka. The second was the Burmese U. N. secretary general U Thant, who held that post from 1961 to 1971. It was he who came here in 1967 and, as an adherent of Buddhism, despaired at seeing the Buddha’s birthplace in a state of disrepair, a wilderness of hyenas and jackals. He went back to New York and set in motion what he called the master plan for Lumbini, which would transform it into a microcosm of the Buddhist world, designed by the renowned Japanese architect Kenzo Tange. Nearly 60 years on, the dream was real. A canal, which Bidari described as “a spinal cord,” ran along a north-south axis, dividing the monastic zones into Mahayana and Theravada. On one side, built in distinctive local styles, are monasteries representing Bhutan, China, Japan, Mongolia, Nepal, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, Tibet and Vietnam. On the other are Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Sri Lanka and Thailand, which along with Bhutan and Mongolia are the world’s only Buddhist-majority nations. A project such as this might easily have fallen prey to being too schematic, a religious theme park of sorts, but that wasn’t the case: It was beautiful and thoughtful, endowed with the spirit of mid-to-late 20th-century Modernism.

Bidari bookended the 2,600-year history of Lumbini with two Asian Buddhists, one from the third century B. C., one from the 20th century A. D. But this is a story whose end would not know its beginning were it not for the work of a handful of European scholars, including the British archaeologist Alexander Cunningham, the first head of the Archaeological Survey of India, who, beginning in the 1830s, used the writings of Chinese travelers like the seventh-century monk Xuanzang to locate and excavate sites such as Sarnath (where Buddha delivered his first sermon) and Bodh Gaya (where he was awakened) in northeastern India. It’s an intellectual debt that still rankles a little. No one wants to be beholden to someone else for their own history. Nor was the role of the West, when it came to Buddhism, a thing of the past. As one grand Tibetan teacher would tell me in Kathmandu, there now existed such a thing as International Western Buddhism. In the West, the Buddha was not only the deity of the lounge, spa and meditation center but also the focus of serious study, of academic departments where Buddhist scholarship was full of vitality.

What made Buddhism so many things to so many people? I received one intriguing answer even before I left New York. At a lecture given by Donald S. Lopez Jr., a scholar of Tibetan Buddhism at the University of Michigan, I asked what the secret of Buddhism’s adaptability was. Lopez said that it lay in the figure of the Buddha himself: “It’s said that when the Buddha speaks to a crowd of thousands of people, every single person there imagines himself sitting alone, and they hear the Buddha speaking to them in their own language, giving a teaching specifically for them.” The Buddha, after all, Lopez added, was often described as the great physician, “and it’s only a quack who prescribes the same medicine to every patient.”

Much was disputed about the Buddha’s life, Bidari explained, but everyone was in agreement that Gautama Buddha was born in Lumbini: It was here, in a garden, that the heavily pregnant Queen Maya, traveling between her husband’s kingdom of Kapilavastu and her maternal home in nearby Devadaha, was overcome by labor pains. (Upon conceiving, she had, in a Buddhist equivalent of the Angel Gabriel appearing to Mary, dreamed that four celestial beings took her to the Himalayas, where a six-tusked white elephant holding a lotus entered her body. Maya would die a week after childbirth, leaving the Buddha to be raised by her sister, notably the first woman convert to the new doctrine, the first bhikshuni, or Buddhist nun.) At the garden in Lumbini, she had clutched at a tree branch and given birth to Siddhartha standing up. Lotuses bloomed as the miraculous child took his first seven steps, whereupon he raised a finger in the air, proclaiming himself “chief of the world” and declaring this birth to be his last. By which he meant that he had arrived at the threshold of that most sought-after state within the Hindu-Buddhist scheme — release from the cycle of reincarnation. “Talk about arrogance!” Naman Ahuja, 51, the chief curator of the Lumbini Museum, would say to me the next morning.

Yet not a trace of that arrogance remained as the boy grew up. As a young man, he subjected himself for six years to the severest forms of Indian penance, until he found these were counterproductive to spiritual advancement. Then, on a full-moon night, after he had eaten some gruel, something of that old assuredness returned to him. He knew precisely when and where — down to the tree under which it would happen — he would battle off the temptations of Mara, god of death and desire, and become the man the Ceylonese art historian Ananda K. Coomaraswamy refers to simply as the Wake. He was 35.

The Buddha didn’t appear out of a vacuum. The ancient Vedas had given his nomadic Indo-Aryan forefathers a song of origin, hymns to the awesome power of nature. To these, starting around 800 B. C., were added the Upanishads, philosophical treatises that were the work of various sages. Their great discovery was that the individual self, with a small “S,” was of the same substance as the Supreme Self, or atman, which, in turn, was identical to the changeless essence of the universe, Brahman. The body tricked us into believing in our own distinctiveness, but really we were connected in essence to all creation and the cosmos. If life had one aim, it was to use the private self as a site of spiritual discovery so as to be rid of the illusion of self. This was moksha, liberation from the cycle of death and rebirth.

Into this world of eternities and essences the Buddha arrived like a wrecking ball, appropriating its terminology but reworking its concepts from the ground up. There was no self, neither individual nor supreme. The world was a blazing river of flux, without beginning or end. In fact, it was this grasping need of ours for stability that was at the root of our ignorance — and, by extension, our suffering. The self was the supreme illusion, the seat of our wish for constancy in a sea of impermanence. It was in order to fortify this illusion that desire, greed and anger rose up in us. The karma, or actions, that we performed in the grip of these impulses left a residue, or trace, that bound us to the wheel of rebirth, preventing us from achieving nirvana — an extinguishment, or release, from the ordeal of having to be born again onto this earth. What we needed above all was to find a mind-born stillness in ourselves within the knowledge that nothing lasts. “Suffering, impermanence, emptiness and no-self,” as the Chinese translator Bill Porter, better known as Red Pine, writes in his travel memoir “Zen Baggage” (2009) — this is the unwavering heart of the dharma; this is what gives the Buddha’s countenance its pitiless smile, that thousand-yard gaze of crushing serenity.

The great physician wasn’t interested in piety, nor even philosophical consistency; he wanted merely to provide the cure for suffering, and he was never more damning than in his silences. His contemporary Mahavira, who revolutionized Jainism, denied the existence of a creator God. The Buddha simply ignored God, not that Hinduism, the tradition both teachers were working out of, had anything resembling the jealous God of Moses or Muhammad. The Buddha cared only about what made life more bearable — and, as one begins to observe his silences on the big questions, it’s possible to feel that in his smiling sagacity lies a contempt for all grand abstractions that do little to alleviate conditions on the ground. Still, the medicine was hard: Our need for anything constant was destined to leave us profoundly unhappy. Consciousness, it was true, was real, but it was nothing to cling to. It rose and fell, like a stream of energy. It was like New York, never kinder to you than when you did not seek to possess it. But if you could entertain the possibility of living within it, without needing to own it, you might experience a kind of release, an unclenching of the fist. The Buddha wouldn’t have countenanced any flirtation with desire (to him, it was like flirting with ignorance), but he would have at least been in partial agreement with Marcel Proust’s shattering realization that “desire makes all things flourish, possession withers them.”

That afternoon with Bidari, I was given a glimpse of how the Buddha’s doctrine could still feel provocative in the land of its birth. Walking down a concourse where monkeys picked nits off one another, we encountered some boys from India who’d come across the open border to see what all the fuss was about. They wore stonewashed jeans and bright-colored shirts in greens and pinks. Something about the ancient site in a foreign country honoring a teacher who was their countryman yet whose doctrine no longer existed in that country unsettled them. Unprovoked, they yelled for all to hear, “Bharat Mata ki Jai, Jai Shri Ram” (“Victory to Mother India, victory to Lord Ram”). Ironically, Ram and Gautama in the Hindu conception were both regarded as incarnations of the great god Vishnu, yet Ram of late had acquired a special status within Hindu nationalism as a politicized deity whose slogans were edged with intolerance and aggression.

Bidari, an elegant gliding figure, sternly admonished the boys, reminding them that they were at a site of Buddhist sanctity — and, moreover, if they wanted to proclaim the greatness of Mother India, they could wait until they had returned home. It was an intriguing moment because it spoke to how the Buddha’s teaching could unnerve, even after centuries. In 1956, the low-caste leader B. R. Ambedkar, a freedom fighter and the father of India’s constitution, had made good on his vow to never die a Hindu. Approaching death, he converted to Buddhism, along with hundreds of thousands of his followers. These neo-Buddhists were the only significant population of Buddhists left in India, barring smaller communities of Buddhists in the Himalayan regions of Ladakh and Himachal Pradesh. What was it that made the doctrine, both then and now, feel so revolutionary?

“Some of its core values,” Ahuja of the Lumbini Museum said to me the next day, when I sat down with him in the restaurant of the town’s Hotel Kasai, “are problematic for those who wish to politically rule through other religions.” Ahuja was no doubt thinking of Hinduism — and caste, especially, which is an ineradicable feature of South Asia’s social organization, not just in India but in Muslim Pakistan no less than in Hindu-Buddhist Nepal. Caste is much more than a social concept; it is a religious idea linked to the purity of the soul. To belong to the priestly caste of Brahmins is not merely to sit atop the social pyramid; it is to have earned that place as a result of one’s karma in a previous life. Here, again, the Buddha was no activist but, in professing that Buddhahood was attainable to all sentient beings, he did more to undermine Brahminism than if he had attacked it directly.

Ahuja had spoken to me of driving up from India to Lumbini through dense forest and, because I would soon be heading to Thailand, where there exists a tradition of forest monks, I asked him about the role of the forest in Hindu-Buddhist myth, art and cosmology. “From the minute the baby is born,” Ahuja said of the historic Buddha, “the forest spirits come out and salute him.” Animism, including a belief in a whole galaxy of sprites, nymphs, serpents and celestial creatures, formed the understructure of belief in old India for both Hinduism and Buddhism. The ability to absorb the forest, with its terrors and wonder, its demons and sages, was like the first test of the new doctrine’s assimilative power. If it could do it here, on home ground, then it could also do it abroad. “Indigenous people, who are forest dwellers and nature worshipers and animistic communities, are easily able to find a way of simultaneously holding on to their pre-existing beliefs while adopting the spiritual teachings of the Buddha,” said Ahuja. Buddhism’s “not forcing you to give up your prior practice.”

WHEN I FIRST arrived in Kathmandu the week before, I’d been struck by the highly distinctive Hindu-inflected Buddhism that prevailed in the capital and its environs. Nepal is an 81 percent Hindu country, but in the Kathmandu Valley, as one young man put it, “the only right answer to the question of whether you’re Hindu or Buddhist is ‘yes.’”

Only a month before my arrival, Gen Z protests against corruption had roiled Kathmandu. Rioters had set fire to the parliament, shopping malls and hotels. I wasn’t sure if it was safe to come. A week on, a journalist friend living there had said all was back to normal. As I took a taxi through Kathmandu at dawn, strips of mountain blue sky overhead, the occasional glimpse of pine-forested hills and Himalayan snows swinging into view, the city exuded the sinister calm that follows a great festival of riot and release. In Thamel, a tourist neighborhood of golden Buddhas, singing bowls and paubhas (traditional Nepali Buddhist paintings), backpackers thronged the streets.

I was staying at the Kathmandu Guest House, whose Buddhist proprietor had the same name as the Nepali monk I’d later meet in Bangkok and the clan to which the historic Buddha belonged: Sakya. It’s said that a massacre at the time of the Buddha had driven the clan north to the Kathmandu Valley, whose culture, language and people are referred to as Newar. The gardens of the guesthouse were like an exercise in competitive pluralism. Here was a shrine to the Hindu god Ganesh; there, a whitewashed stupa and, on a pedestal at the center of the lawn, a vajra, the double-headed ritual scepter that’s the mark of the kind of Vajrayana, or Tantric, Buddhism practiced in the valley, as well as across the Himalayas.

Tantrism is shrouded in secrecy — hidden rites, rituals, shrines and deities — operating out of the logic that not every practice is for everyone. If Theravada, with its checklist of monastic rules, is a great leveler, Tantric Buddhism creates a kind of aristocracy in which secret practices are reserved for certain individuals who display special capacities, usually as a result of having been someone grander in a previous life, such as a Rinpoche, who is often thought to be the descendant of a previous master. Within this world, lineage was not a matter of birth but rather of spiritual rebirth.

A young employee of the guesthouse spoke of secret rites that her family performed, secret idols; her boss spoke of hidden rooms in Buddhist temples; and, later that morning, when Birat Raj Bajracharya, a 29-year-old Buddhist scholar, showed up to take me to a temple outside Kathmandu “with an esoteric character,” the question that was uppermost in my mind was how I was going to see this vein of the dharma in action when it seemed to operate in what one friend described as “a prison of secrecy.”

As we set out on Bajracharya’s motorbike for Bajrayogini Temple, he suggested we stop at a monastery in Thamel where the Bengali abbot Atisha, who was instrumental in bringing the second wave of Buddhism to Tibet, stayed awhile in the 11th century before heading north. Nothing about the story of the dharma’s movement along trade routes — silk in the north, cotton and maritime in the south via monks, armed with icons and manuscripts, hitching rides with merchants and traders — is linear. Imagine a pinball ricocheting back and forth across Asia for 25 centuries. Nor are the lines between the different schools as ironclad as they can seem now. The strains that would eventually take hold in Southeast Asia — the ones that traveled via Sri Lanka — are sometimes referred to as the Southern Transmission and retained something of the spirit of early Buddhism, whereas the more esoteric strains that traveled north to China, Korea, Japan, Mongolia and Tibet are the beneficiaries of the last gasp of Buddhist thought in India. These transmissions today look immutable, but they were in fact much more fluid, with Southeast Asia once being replete with Tantric Buddhism, and with precursors of Theravada, such as Sthaviravada, active in Nepal and other northern societies. The passage of time hardens the relationship between a particular region and its brand of Buddhism, seeming to suggest an integral link between the two, but this is a kind of historical illusion that makes it as hard for us to imagine a Tantric Thailand as a Roman Catholic Britain.

Then there are the ghost lands of Buddhism: Muslim societies such as Indonesia, Afghanistan, Pakistan and Uzbekistan where Buddhism once flourished but where now only suggestive ruins remain, such as the stunning complex of stupas with their latticed domes at Borobudur on Java in Indonesia, or the foundations of Taxila, a once-great Buddhist university outside of Islamabad in Pakistan. Most haunting of all are the now-empty alcoves at Bamiyan in Afghanistan, in which Buddha colossi stood for some 1,500 years until the Taliban blew them up in 2001.

Atisha was both a student and a scholar at Vikramshila university, in modern-day Bihar, India, which the forces of a Turkic general destroyed in 1193. The invasions devastated India as a whole, but it remains a mystery why Hinduism survived while Buddhism was wiped out. The British scholar David L. Snellgrove offers one compelling explanation in “Buddhist Himalaya” (1957). Buddhism, he writes, “relied always upon the existence of an elite, who were contemplatives and scholars. Since these always congregated in monasteries, the destruction of these places was sufficient to bring the doctrine to an end. But Hinduism is the whole traditional life of India, social and religious.”

After the collapse of Buddhism in India, the Kathmandu Valley became a petri dish for Buddhist art and ideas. Standing in the darkened hallway of the monastery in Thamel, gazing through a wooden lattice at a courtyard of votive stupas, Bajracharya ran me through some of the things that made Newar Buddhism distinct. It had a system of hereditary monk-householders who were permitted to marry, and who spent some symbolic amount of time performing the rites of the temple associated with their family. The language of the sacred scripture was not Pali, as it was for Southern Buddhism, but Sanskrit. Bajracharya himself grew up around both Hindu and Buddhist rites. Despite his ponytail and motorbike, he had a solemn, scholarly mien. “I decided at the age of 18,” he said, “that for me personally, my path to salvation was through the Buddha.”

After a quick lunch, we careened through Kathmandu streets and headed for the dark furrowed hills. Occasionally we’d stop at the burned-out remains of a shopping mall or hotel draped in green netting. At the Bajrayogini Temple, a fierce form of the Hindu deity Shiva, known as Mahakala in Buddhism, kept guard. Bajracharya and I strolled down to see his representation as a dark slab of triangular rock, serpent-hooded and streaked with vermilion. Farther up the wooded path, a friend of Bajracharya’s, Prawjol, who belongs to the same priestly caste as him, was fulfilling his duties to the goddess Bajrayogini. The tantric energy of the site was already strong, but Bajracharya’s friend seemed to play it up for two female pilgrims from Taiwan. “In the West,” he said, standing in the gold door of the temple, dressed in a red tunic, his white pajama covered in carmine powder, “who flies in the sky on a broomstick?”

“Witches,” I answered dutifully.

“Exactly!” he exclaimed. Pointing to one of the goddesses represented in the precincts of the temple, he said, “She used to feast on babies, but she gave that up for the Buddha. She’s here now to protect the dharma.” As Prawjol spoke, I found myself struggling to articulate what made something tantric. The word had acquired an unserious salacious connotation in the West yet, like all good clichés, it wasn’t entirely off the mark. The tantras themselves are principally secret texts, which produced a range of practices. Two years earlier, I’d stood in a necropolis at Mount Koya in Japan, which a ninth-century monk had made the home of Shingon Buddhism, and felt the same darkling energy I felt now. I had seen it among desert saints on the edge of the Gobi in Mongolia; I had felt its presence in various strands of Hinduism, especially those related to Shiva the Destroyer. The aim was for certain individuals to develop powers and abilities that could ultimately be put in service of the common good but were too exalted and, frankly, dangerous to be made available to the laity.

At certain times, such as the next morning at the Swayambhunath Stupa, a vast Buddhist complex connected with the creation myth of the Kathmandu Valley, the tantric element could seem almost like a parody of itself. I was with Swosti Rajbhandari Kayastha, 51, a scholar of Nepali art and culture. Walking up to the stupa among a swarm of pilgrims, Kayastha pointed to the Shantipur Temple on our left. “It’s been said that they have a book written in snake’s blood,” she said, making me laugh at how much Tantrism lived up to its reputation for sorcery and black magic. “When there was a drought in the valley, the king would bring it out and expose it to sunlight, which would alleviate the drought.” The presence of magic, often transmuted into physical entities such as amulets and talismans, or superstition, was an ineradicable aspect of religion. Yet it was precisely this element, including mindless ritual, that the Buddha, as well as Ashoka, had inveighed against. Ahuja had cited how, in inscription after inscription, the great Buddhist emperor was “pleading with the society to stop performing these rituals,” especially since their performance invariably placed them in the hands of a priestly caste and undid the most conspicuous advantage of the Buddha’s teaching, namely that all sentient beings are capable of Buddhahood and do not need a priest to help them get there. It was this same dual impulse, in part the eradication of magic and superstition, in part the abolition of religious middlemen, that underlay Christ’s conflict with the Pharisees, or Muhammad’s clearing of the Kaaba of idols in 630 when he entered Mecca in triumph. Each of these founders had been a threat because they returned religion to the hands of the people but, in each of these religions, that human need to put our faith in spells and juju, in lucky charms and, most of all, in other human beings with a direct line to the Almighty or to some eternal truth, had undermined what made these new doctrines revolutionary in the first place.

Where the stupa now stood, Kayastha explained that Manjushri, the bodhisattva of wisdom, who is said to reside at Mount Wutai in China, had seen a shining blue lotus appear over an ancient lake. He drew his sword and cut a gorge, allowing the water to drain away and the Kathmandu Valley to become inhabitable. The stupa was thought to enfold the lotus within its dome. This emphasis on bodhisattvas, which are human representations of Buddhist ideals, is among the simplest ways to differentiate Mahayana and Vajrayana from Theravada, in which they play a smaller role.

The gods were in full force that morning at Swayambhunath, where a euphoric atmosphere of alpine devotion prevailed. Pilgrims carried baskets that looked like hair or wool but were so many wicks doused in oil, an offering called lakh batti, or “a hundred thousand lights.” People did this, Kayastha explained, to commemorate a dead family member or mark an important bit of luck or success.

One of the things that made Swayambhunath distinct, Kayastha said, was that Vairocana — the Buddha of sunyata, or “emptiness” — who is normally inside a stupa, was on the outside here, as were the four other celestial Buddhas and their spouses, including Amitabha, symbolizing infinite light, who was a central figure in the Pure Land Buddhism I’d encounter in Taiwan. Each represented an attainment of the perfection of wisdom, and each was clad in brocade and fineries. It was impossible to know who among the pilgrims were Hindu, who Buddhist. One was so enraptured that, lighting a lamp with his eyes closed, he set fire to Kayastha’s hair, which we managed to put out just in time. As we came to a long staircase leading down from the stupa, Kayastha showed me a stone plinth on which the vajra sat. Below were the animals of the Chinese zodiac. “What were they doing there?” she asked rhetorically — as if their presence were an unsolved mystery.

DURING MY TIME in Nepal, I made several trips to the Golden Temple in Patan, a beautifully preserved city within greater Kathmandu that has many fine examples of Newar Buddhist architecture, with its use of intricate brickwork and heavily carved dark wooden screens. The temple itself was a jewel, housing an exquisite green statue of Tara, the Mother of all Buddhas, representing the female principle, with its equal measures of compassion and ferocity. It also held one of the grandest texts of the entire Buddhist canon: a more than 900-year-old manuscript, written out in gold, of the Prajnaparamita, the Perfection of Wisdom. This seminal 8,000-verse treatise on emptiness was among the texts that the monk Xuanzang took back to China and translated in the seventh century.

At the closing ceremony one evening, I watched a young boy in a lamp-lit courtyard of gold pagodas beat the gambashin, a cylindrical wooden log, 108 times to banish our 108 defilements, which include mental impurities and earthly desires. That number had traveled as far east as Japan, so that on New Year’s Eve the country’s temple bells were struck 108 times.

The Sakya clan balanced the demands of their ancestry with those of the modern world. Sujeev Sakya, 58, who is a management consultant and writer, told me one evening in Patan, over Nepali Scotch and the most deliciously spiced potatoes, known as Mustang aloo, “that if there was one religion for the middle classes, it was Buddhism.” I laughed. “No, seriously,” he continued. Islam and Christianity were for the downtrodden; Hinduism was unabashedly hierarchical. Buddhism alone, with its rich history of merchant patronage, spoke to the demands and desires of materialism in the modern world.

Yet Newar Buddhism, the indigenous variant practiced in the Kathmandu Valley, suffered as a consequence of its distinctly Hindu character. Even within the Buddhist fold in Nepal, other schools such as Theravada and Tibetan Buddhism were gaining ground. On one of my last days in Kathmandu, I met a senior Tibetan Rinpoche, whom some described as “Yoda-like,” given to cryptic utterances, at his mountain retreat. When I asked Chokyi Nyima Rinpoche, 75, dressed in an ocher tunic and a maroon shamtap, or skirt, about the tension between the transmissions of Buddhism, he responded firmly. “When you look at a tree,” he said, “you don’t concentrate on its different branches. You try and see the tree as a whole.” It felt to me like the magnanimity of the winning side. Not only did Tibetan Buddhism have glamorous converts like Richard Gere and Robert Thurman (the father of Uma, and the first American ordained as a Tibetan Buddhist monk), it was also at the forefront of the relationship between religion and modernity. One of Rinpoche’s Danish disciples would be attending a conference in Taiwan in a few weeks about the convergence of artificial intelligence and religion. I wondered if Tibetan Buddhism had taken flight the way it had precisely because it had been released from two kinds of bonds: the first was not having to live alongside Hinduism as a parent religion, the second was the loss of a homeland in Tibet, which made instant cosmopolitans of figures like the Dalai Lama. The spiritual and temporal leader of Tibetan Buddhists had acquired so great a cult status in the West that one might be forgiven for thinking he represented all of Buddhism. He had appeared in Apple ads and oversaw a shrewd publicity machine but, above all, he was a captivating personality, full of charm, intelligence and humility, which made him an excellent ambassador.

I wanted to know about Rinpoche’s life in Tibet. He described it as a place where the flowers were so bright they were blinding, and a certain kindness and trust existed among people. He also evoked its forbidding geography, which had perhaps left the transmission there whole and pure in ways that could never have been true of Nepal, which was a crucible of cross-fertilization.

Hinduism and Buddhism had merged inextricably in the Kathmandu Valley, but whereas for the former assimilation was a victory, for the latter it was death. One of the most powerful examples of this symbiosis in Kathmandu was the figure of the kumari, a living goddess, who was chosen from a Buddhist family in order to serve as the human incarnation of the Hindu deity Taleju.

One morning, in a neighborhood of alleyways, courtyards and temples, I met Mattina Shakya. She had been the valley’s chief kumari until 2017 — there are as many as a dozen in Nepal — when the onset of puberty brought her term to an end. A child singled out on the basis of certain physical attributes to live as a goddess, Shakya grew up in a special kumari house on Durbar Square, or Royal Square, performing a whole range of ceremonial functions. At festival time, she was carried through the streets, her feet never allowed to touch the ground. Seeing her now in her drab bedroom, with a picture of her in full regalia against the pistachio-colored walls behind her — her lips red, her face white, her eyes elongated with kohl, a third eye painted on to her forehead — I felt I was in the presence of a fading star of silent cinema. Except Shakya, now pursuing a degree in business administration, was only 19. A new kumari, her 3-year-old cousin, had just been selected. Was it difficult to adjust to normal life, having started out as a goddess, I asked her. She was cripplingly shy. “Yes, it was hard at first,” she said, but the joys of being reunited with her family were a great consolation.

Listening to her speak, I wondered if the persistence of Nepal’s living traditions, like its prisons of lineage and secrecy, made Newar Buddhism too culturally specific, too much an addendum to Hinduism and, as a result, too untranslatable. I began to see, especially as I went farther east, that Buddhism’s rupture from the environment where it had emerged represented a moment of intellectual freedom. It unshackled the doctrine from the burden of cultural particularity, giving it an inner life of its own and endowing it with a preternatural power to travel.

I started my Buddhist journey last October at the birthplace of the Buddha in Lumbini, near the frontier of modern-day India and Nepal. I was intrigued by the fact it was a place of pilgrimage for nearly a thousand years, attracting monks, scholars and kings from every corner of the Buddhist world, before totally vanishing from view for centuries. To me, this lost locus of Buddhist sanctity was like a metaphor for the disappearance of Buddhism from India, the land of its birth and development, and the country where I had grown up. I wanted to know why Buddhism was abandoned there yet flourished in so many other places.

Production: Ashok Pahari

‘Quite Brutal,’ ‘Not Friendly’: What People in China Say of Trump

The New York Times May 14, 2026

Trump-Xi Summit

Advertisement

Supported by

Residents in four Chinese cities described a mixture of amusement and anger, blaming U. S. tensions for a slowing economy and rising fuel prices.

By Ana Swanson

Ana Swanson covers international trade. She spent the week in China, reporting from four cities around the country.

Even for everyday people in China, President Trump’s influence looms large.

A steel trader in the southern city of Fuzhou said his business had been depressed by the trade war. A taxi driver in northern China complained that the increase in global gas prices amid the war in Iran meant he had to pay more at the pump.

At a shopping mall in Beijing, Sunny Sun, a woman who was invested in stocks, said she was watching her portfolio, wary of the impact of announcements from the president’s summit with Xi Jinping, the Chinese leader.

“There’s definitely some uncertainty in the market sentiment, because Trump is the kind of person who says one thing today and another tomorrow when he gets back to the United States,” Ms. Sun said. “His words can actually stir up things globally.”

Some residents were surprised to hear that Mr. Trump was visiting China, but all knew who he was. They cited his attempted assassination, his business record, his refusal to wear face masks during the pandemic, his campaign against Iran, and, of course, his tariffs.

“He’s a rather interesting person,” said Milly Zhu, a 34-year-old who works in film and TV promotion and was walking in a shopping mall in Beijing. “Some of his words and actions, for example regarding China, seem like stand-up comedy to people in China,” she said.

“Our President Xi might be considered, in comparison to Trump, more serious,” she added.

Often, their views were negative. Yang Saixiang, a 47-year old worker at a nail salon in a shopping mall in Fuzhou, said the Iran war had worsened her views and that many Chinese people disliked Mr. Trump.

“He’s not friendly to China,” she said. She said tariffs and the U. S.-China trade war had dampened earnings for her customers, and she questioned why the United States could not simply change presidents. “I think at his age, he doesn’t need to be president anymore,” she said.

Peng Shuiming, an 18-year-old hairdresser who sat outside the Fuzhou mall playing games on his phone, said the war with Iran had further soured his opinion on the United States, which was already poor.

“My impression of him isn’t very good; he’s quite brutal,” he said of Mr. Trump.

Mr. Peng said he was indifferent to Mr. Trump’s visit, and that whether China needed the United States was a “matter of choice. I feel China is quite powerful,” he said.

Zhang Lei, a 40-year-old taxi driver in Jinan, Shandong Province, argued that China was already wealthy, with little need for foreign goods, and that it should be more assertive.

“The fact that he’s taking the initiative to visit China means that China can control him, right?” he said of Mr. Trump. “It means that this trade war isn’t just unsuccessful for China, it means that the U. S. is also struggling.”

Some of the negative views of the United States appeared to be based on misinformation circulated on social media. One woman cited a report that beggars in the United States eat human flesh, while Mr. Peng mentioned that his view on the United States had worsened after seeing a report during the pandemic about the United States dumping bodies in the sea.

Others seemed to blame Mr. Trump and the trade war for broader weakness in the Chinese economy, some of which was likely linked to the current real estate downturn, or other reasons.

Chen Gang, a 42-year-old steel trader in Fuzhou, said tense relations between the United States and China were hurting his business. He sells steel to the construction industry, but the sector is shrinking.

“It would be better to avoid tariff wars and just cooperate amicably, without all this back and forth,” he said.

Mr. Chen said that Chinese leaders should be “polite and courteous” to Mr. Trump — at least on the surface. “People say nice things on the surface, but what they really mean behind the scenes is another matter. That’s how it is in business,” he said.

Many expressed hope that the meetings between Mr. Trump and Mr. Xi would set the United States and China on a more stable path. Almost all characterized China as inherently peaceful.

“We don’t want war, we want peace,” Ms. Zhu said. “We want to get along well with the United States, and we want to develop our economy. Only peace can create a better economy.”

In Jinan, the northern Chinese city, Shen Jianmin, a 74-year-old retiree and former farmer who was relaxing in a public plaza on Wednesday, said that Mr. Trump tended to stir up trouble for no reason. But he said the visit was a positive development.

“It’s good that the U. S. is coming to China, right?” he said. “The friendship between the two countries is good.”

“Everyone wants a good life; which ordinary person wants to fight? When you’re constantly at war, it’s the ordinary people who suffer,” he added.

Li You contributed research.

Ana Swanson covers trade and international economics for The Times and is based in Washington. She has been a journalist for more than a decade.

In a City of Big Dreams, Many Young Adults See a Cloudy Future

The New York Times May 14, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

A bleak job market. Rising rents. Huge debt. In New York and other cities, traditional milestones of adulthood feel further away for some 20- and 30-year-olds.

By Troy Closson

Troy Closson, who covers young people, spoke to more than two dozen young adults, economists, work force leaders and career coaches in New York City.

It was around No. 87 when Soban Ali started to lose track of all his job applications.

He had moved to New York City, eager to start life away from the Washington area, where he was born and raised. But seven months after arriving, he was laid off from his job at a federal contractor during last fall’s government shutdown. So he started a spreadsheet: “The Great Job Hunt of 2025.”

He applied to roughly 450 openings. He landed upward of 10 interviews. He still doesn’t have a full-time job.

Now, Mr. Ali, 24, feels guilty telling friends he can’t join them for dinner. He wants to start a family one day, but worries. “I can’t even afford myself, so how am I going to afford someone else?” he said. And he laments that he can’t pursue some of the hobbies that have always brought him joy, such as hip-hop dance. Classes are too expensive: about $25.

“It’s this existential depression and existential dread of, ‘What am I going to do with my life?’” said Mr. Ali, who earns $18 an hour working part-time at an after-school program. That’s just $1 more per hour than minimum wage.

He wonders about five years from now: “Am I going to be making a good, livable income? Or am I going to be flipping burgers?”

It’s a rough time to be a young adult. Young college-degree holders face their worst spring in the U. S. job market since the coronavirus pandemic.

And if headwinds are blowing across the United States, they can feel like gale-force squalls in New York, one of the world’s most notoriously expensive cities.

Rents here are surging faster than in the rest of the country. Postings for entry-level jobs in New York City plummeted by more than 37 percent between 2022 and 2024. And student loan debt is rising: In no state do young adults between 25 and 34 hold more average debt at almost $38,000.

Mark Levine, the city comptroller, summed it up.

“Young people are facing a triple whammy.”

New York’s allure is unmatched. The city attracted more college graduates between 2021 and 2024 than Los Angeles and Chicago combined. About one in four New Yorkers — or more than 2.1 million residents — are between 18 and 34 years old.

That popularity as a landing spot helps foster the city’s competitive hiring market.

Today’s job market is nowhere as rough for young adults as it was during the Great Recession in the late 2000s or the depths of the pandemic. But the city’s unemployment rate for 22- to 27-year-olds with a college degree has risen to about 7.3 percent, slightly higher than for peers with no degree — and higher than national rates for their age group.

Those numbers fail to capture those who are stuck in low-paying work that doesn’t use their credentials — like Natalie Lui, a finance and marketing graduate who went from being an I. T. analyst at an investment bank to working part-time at a gym’s front desk.

Ms. Lui estimated that she has applied to at least 300 full-time positions. She put a call-out on TikTok: “please comment literally ANY and most effective ways to get a job in NYC. PLS HELP A GIRL OUT.”

“It took a lot out of me to even post that online,” said Ms. Lui, who turns 26 this summer and worries about affording health coverage after she’s kicked off her family plan. “But it’s come to that.”

In interviews, many young adults said that they felt lost at a moment when the path to a comfortable life appears filled with fresh obstacles.

The traditional milestones of adulthood — marriage, financial independence, living without roommates — seem ever more distant. And many young adults feel burned out by knowing that their résumés may never be read by a person and that artificial intelligence could upend the skills needed to succeed.

“I’m trying to figure out what it is: Is it an experience thing?” asked Mirko Mormile, 27, a Brooklyn College alumnus who was raised in the Bensonhurst neighborhood and studied business. He is a full-time digital content creator — “not entirely by choice,” he said — after applying to other work over the past year.

“Is it, am I not good enough?” said Mr. Mormile, who is living with his grandfather, helping to care for him after a fall.

The growing angst among young adults has led to crowdfunding pleas on GoFundMe and inspired punchlines for stand-up routines.

“I left my job this year, and I moved to New York cause I wanted to try unemployment on the most difficult level,” one comedian, Josh Martier, quipped during a recent set.

“Let me tell you, that city has not disappointed.”

One 22-year-old said that she arrived in New York last year with her cat and a suitcase, dog-sitting in exchange for housing. She couldn’t find work in Chicago after dropping out of college.

She had applied to more than 1,000 jobs, from marketing openings to positions at Trader Joe’s and Starbucks, but couldn’t get in the door. She worked as a stripper, but business was slow. So she began sex work.

Many of her friends are unemployed. One joined the military because he couldn’t find other work, and was recently deployed to Bahrain. “That’s just what our generation is,” she said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss her sex work.

“I feel like no one cares.”

But let’s say you succeed in finding a well-paying job. Congratulations: The reward is a cost of living crisis that devours your paychecks.

Utility bills are rising, and food prices in the New York City area surged by 56 percent between 2012 and 2022, faster than in the rest of the nation. The cost of a Citi Bike membership jumped by 41 percent during the past six years.

And a large cup of coffee can push $7 after tax.

“Even just the little things that young people find joy in aren’t really affordable anymore,” said Rosaury Valenzuela, 30, an alumna of City College of New York who lost her job with a nonprofit organization in October and has struggled to find listings that offer a living wage.

She misses simple conveniences, like buying food at a single grocery store. Now, she needs to visit four, shopping around for low prices. And she said that it feels like the cost of a night out in the city has tripled — or quadrupled.

For Ms. Valenzuela and many others, housing costs are also a burning issue as rents rise quicker than wages.

The apartment hunt is especially suffocating in a city where — as Eric Kober, a senior fellow at the Manhattan Institute, put it — “the system is very much stacked against young adults,” with limited vacancies and few affordable options.

Carla Marie Davis, 34, a digital content creator born and raised in Brooklyn, has sometimes spent well over half her income on rent. She wanted to live alone but couldn’t find a budget-friendly studio or one-bedroom rental in or near her neighborhood, Bedford-Stuyvesant.

So she looked into homeownership through the city’s affordable co-ops for lower-income residents and discovered that she needed far more assets to qualify. It took two years to find a co-op in her price range.

“It shouldn’t take the stars aligning perfectly and having all the luck in the world,” she said, grateful for the newfound stability. Her parents had already moved to Atlanta to live more comfortably, and she was “nearly pushed to the point of leaving” herself a few years ago.

Perhaps no American city is defined by its trade-offs quite like New York. Tight living quarters and eye-popping prices are the cost of living in a dynamic metropolis.

But some work force leaders fear that today’s tribulations threaten to prevent young native New Yorkers from staying and dissuade all but the wealthiest transplants from settling.

They say it would be a blow to the city’s culture and economy. Already, residents between 26 and 35 are twice as likely to move out as the rest of the population.

Among them was Gabriel Perez Silva, a 29-year-old photographer who recently left for Burbank, Calif., after more than seven years in New York. He traded a Brooklyn apartment whose bathroom he said was “crashing in on itself” for more work opportunities and better value. He’s closer to a park and even has a hot tub.

“My quality of life has completely skyrocketed,” he said.

Yet Mr. Perez Silva and other young adults still saw the city’s charm.

Deanna Richards, 27, aspires to act on Broadway, but had to put her aspirations on hold and prioritize stability after facing two bouts of unemployment within six months last year. She shares a roughly $1,000-a-month rent-controlled apartment with her boyfriend, and said she would not be able to survive without it.

Still, she relishes the city’s arts scene and industrious spirit: “It helps push me in moments where I’m like, ‘Oh my gosh, what am I doing?’ ”

I spoke with more than two dozen young adults, economists and workforce leaders for this story who agreed: It’s rough out there. It has never been easy for 20- and 30-year-olds to start their adult lives. But for many, this moment feels like the New York dream of making it here — or nowhere — is slipping further away.

@Troy Closson it's rough, too, for our 30-something family member who lost his job at the end of 2019 and has never fully recovered. With a few substantive 6 month contract gigs, used up savings and what appeared to be a stable full-time job that lasted only a year. It's been brutal. Lots of interviews, even second interviews and then rejected or ghosted.

Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

Troy Closson is a reporter for The Times covering children, teenagers and young adults in New York City.

Can Some Very Tiny Particles Cool the Planet? One Tech Company Says Yes.

The New York Times May 14, 2026

Stardust Solutions says its tiny spheres can reflect the sun’s rays without harming people or the environment. Critics say private companies have no business altering Earth’s atmosphere.

An enclosed test chamber at Stardust Solutions, an Israeli tech company that says can help cool the planet by reflecting sunlight away from the Earth. Credit...

Supported by

By Eric Niiler

A company at the forefront of solar geoengineering — the notion that blocking radiation from the sun could cool a warming planet — has disclosed details of the materials it wants to sprinkle in the atmosphere.

Stardust Solutions, led by former members of Israel’s nuclear energy program, is publishing research on Thursday that reveals the chemical properties of its particles, how they would affect the atmosphere and how high-flying aircraft would disperse the material.

The privately held company, founded in 2023, is farthest ahead in the contest to take an idea that was once the stuff of science fiction and move it into the mainstream. It has attracted $75 million from investors, has applied for a patent and is submitting its research to scientific journals for peer review.

Its chief executive, Yanai Yedvab, said Stardust Solutions had only tested its materials in its laboratory and had no plans to conduct outdoor tests. Outdoor trials would only be done in collaboration with a government that would set ground rules and guardrails, he said in an interview.

As humans continue to burn fossil fuels and greenhouse gas emissions reach record levels, Dr. Yedvab and others say that managing solar radiation deserves serious consideration.

“This is a very powerful tool that will be ready for testing very soon, and we want policymakers to start thinking seriously, ‘What will it take in practice?’” he said.

But the idea of manipulating the atmosphere to turn down the temperature of the Earth remains contentious, and more than 600 scientists and academics have called for an international ban.

Prakash Kashwan, a professor of environmental studies at Brandeis University, is among them. He said solar geoengineering could tamper with weather patterns, damaging food production and local economies.

It’s especially worrisome for residents of South Asia and parts of East Africa and Latin America who rely on yearly monsoon rainfall to irrigate crops, Dr. Kashwan said.

“There’s this social risk for at least two billion people that is directly connected to the lack of scientific understanding about how interfering with the global temperature thermostat is going to interfere with the monsoon formation,” he said. “We don’t have a solution for those kinds of risks.”

Tennessee and Florida have banned geoengineering and, in February, Representative Greg Steube, a Florida Republican, introduced a bill in Congress that would do the same. In 2023, at the direction of Congress, the Biden administration issued a report on the need to study solar geoengineering. That research that has not been pursued by the Trump administration.

Dr. Yedvab said that Stardust officials were having preliminary conversations with policymakers in the United States and Europe about the company’s proposal but declined to identify them. Stardust Solutions spent $370,000 last year on federal lobbyists, according to OpenSecrets, which tracks lobbying spending.

The materials produced by Stardust are made from amorphous silica, which is used as a food additive and in some consumer products, and calcium carbonate, a compound found in eggshells and limestone. The company said its particles were biodegradable, were not harmful to people or animals, and would not accumulate in the oceans or soil. Released in the upper atmosphere, the particles could reflect a small amount of sunlight away from Earth, the company said.

Until Thursday, the company kept the ingredients under wraps, requiring anyone who wanted to see its data to sign a nondisclosure agreement.

Michael S. Diamond, a professor of meteorology at Florida State University, said he was surprised by the simplicity of the Stardust particle.

“It’s quite an elegant idea, and I like that it is using relatively well known particles,” said Dr. Diamond, who studies how aerosol particles affect the climate. “I’m a little bit surprised that they’ve kept this so secretive. I thought they were going to do something really out there, but amorphous silica itself is a very widely used product.”

David Keith, professor of geophysical sciences at the University of Chicago who has researched the idea of slowing climate change with reflective particles for more than two decades, said he needed more information.

“This is really good idea, it’s cool and it might be useful,” Dr. Keith said. “But the big question is, what is this environmental impact? The answer has to be, from anybody, is that we don’t know.”

Dr. Yedvab likened his company to a drug development lab that conducted its initial work behind closed doors before applying for approval from the Food and Drug Administration.

“Solar reflection technology is heavy lift,” Dr. Yedvab said during an interview. “You want to make sure that you’re doing it when you can say credibly. You don’t want to say, ‘Yeah, I overlooked something or something was missing and I need to go back and correct it.’ This was the responsible thing to do.”

In addition to concerns about unintended consequences, environmental groups have worried that geoengineering could reduce pressure on countries and industries to reduce the emissions that are driving climate change. But in the past several years, record global temperatures, increasing risk of drought and wildfire, and the increasing intensity of severe storms and floods, have pushed many researchers and some environmentalists to accept the notion that solar geoengineering must at least be studied.

Dozens of academic labs in the United States, Europe, and Asia are now modeling how spraying various amounts of reflective particles in different locations might cool the planet. A team from the University of Cambridge and Harvard University, with backing from the British government, plans to launch a high-altitude drone sometime next year to test reflective particles in a metal tray without releasing them into the atmosphere.

Most of these efforts have contemplated using sulfur dioxide, a compound released during volcanic eruptions that changes from a gas to sulfate, an aerosol particle that reflects sunlight. Because sulfate particles in some concentrations can damage the protective ozone layer, and because they might warm the stratosphere, Stardust officials said they chose something different.

Stardust Solutions is registered in Delaware as a U. S. company with an Israeli subsidiary called Stardust Labs. Its laboratory is in Ness Ziona, Israel, about 12 miles south of Tel Aviv, near the renowned Weizmann Institute of Science.

Dr. Yedvab, co-founder Amyad Spector and a team of 25 researchers have developed two kinds of particles. The first is made of amorphous silica and coated in a material to prevent it from interacting with atmospheric gases. The second particle is a shell of amorphous silica around an inner core of calcium carbonate.

The company said the amorphous silica would be used as in initial effort to reflect up to 1 percent of the coming sunlight, while the silica-carbonate particle could be used at higher concentrations to block more than 1 percent.

Using a chamber that mimics the subzero conditions of the stratosphere, Stardust researchers tested the silica particle with atmospheric trace gases to see how they would react.

The second silica-carbonate particle has similar surface chemistry to the first one but is still being tested, Dr. Yedvab said.

Stardust also tested a dispersion system to make sure the particles would spread out after being sprayed from an aircraft and would not react with water vapor to form ice crystals and drop toward the ground.

Stardust executives said that initial effort to begin atmospheric cooling would cost about $10 billion. That would cover the material, the aircraft that could disperse it at high altitudes and a monitoring system using a chemical tag to track the particles in the air and, later, on the ground.

By adding 10 million tons of the reflective particles to the atmosphere over the course of several years, the atmosphere could be cooled by 1.5 degrees Celsius, the company said. There are no known health effects from exposure to amorphous silica at the levels found in the environment or in commercial products, according to the Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry, a branch of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. But some scientists said they wanted more information about how the particles might affect human respiratory health.

Dr. Yedvab noted that the Department of Homeland Security sprayed amorphous silica into the New York City subway system in 2016 as part of an experiment to test emergency preparedness against a potential bioterrorism attack. The silica was used as a nontoxic tracer to check how a potential pathogen might spread in the subway.

Still, the conflict between Stardust and some critics is not over the safety of its particles but whether a private company should be involved in geoengineering research at all and Stardust’s lack of transparency until now.

Daniele Visioni, professor of earth and atmospheric sciences at Cornell University, said Stardust should follow the traditional path of announcing scientific discoveries by presenting data at a conference and answering questions from scientists working in the same field.

“I keep seeing that all the moves they make are the wrong ones process-wise,” Dr. Visioni said.

The American Geophysical Union, the Natural Resources Defense Council and two other nonprofit groups have formed a coalition to write a code of ethics for research into cooling the planet.

Shuchi Talati, who founded the coalition, said she was troubled by the idea that a private for-profit company could own the rights to a something that could profoundly affect the planet.

“There’s no trust whatsoever,” Dr. Talati said. “Where has the scientific merit review and the transparent public review process been for the last two years for this alleged particle? This idea of intellectual property with solar radiation management is massively problematic.”

Dr. Yedvab said that research into geoengineering had been stalled and that Stardust was shaking things up. “We feel that our role is to disrupt this field to make sure that governments have options,” he said.

What Are Your Evening Rituals? We Want to Know.

The New York Times May 14, 2026

Advertisement

Do you meditate? Play Wordle? Wear soft pajamas and sip chamomile tea? We’d like to hear about the little routines that help you wind down.

By Amanda Schupak

Some nights before I fall asleep, my husband invites me over to his side of the bed so we can review the funny Instagram posts he’s saved for me during the week. We giggle at memes and videos of dogs wearing silly costumes, and revel in the nostalgia of ’90s alternative rock.

As a sleep reporter, I understand the potential issues that may result from screen use before bed — like staying up too late or coming across content that may lead to anxiety. But I don’t worry about breaking this hallowed sleep hygiene rule. The laughter and closeness with my husband relaxes me, and it’s a routine we both look forward to. (The research on blue light’s effects on sleep is murky, anyway.)

Most of us have little rituals or evening habits that signal that the day is done and that it’s time for rest. Some people meditate. Others listen to audiobooks or read physical books aloud to their partners. Some may complete elaborate skin care routines or do the dishes so that they wake up to a clean kitchen.

We want to know: What do you do right before bed?

Everyone at the Musk v. Altman Trial Is Using Fancy Butt Cushions

Wired May 13, 2026

The final stragglers testified on Wednesday in the Musk v. Altman trial. The witnesses generated few waves, aside from the revelation that Microsoft has so far spent over $100 billion on its partnership with OpenAI. Rather than focus on that, I wanted to bring you a candid observation that my colleague Maxwell Zeff and I can’t stop talking about after spending nearly three weeks watching the trial.

The courtroom is littered with butt cushions.

Several of the hard, wooden benches on the right side of US district Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers’ courtroom are reserved for OpenAI and Microsoft’s attorneys, executives, and other members of the defense. About 10 people, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and general counsel Che Chang, have benefitted from thick black cushions—the plushest of them from the brand Purple; $120 from Target—that spare their butts from hours of sitting. Some cushions have rounded corners, while others are square. On Wednesday, Chang even put one behind his back, a less common but not unprecedented move in the courtroom.

OpenAI President Greg Brockman and his wife, Anna, have watched a considerable portion of the trial—and have both been prolific users of pristine white pillows. Judging from the tags bursting from the seams, the pillows seem to be from the sleeping goods brand Coop, which sells a two pack of alternative down-filled throw pillows for $35.

On Wednesday, an OpenAI bodyguard carried a purple handbag into the courtroom, with a pillow for each of the Brockmans. Anna gave her husband just a minute to suffer in pillow-less oblivion before she discreetly passed one to him and then situated her own. I felt bad for OpenAI chief futurist Joshua Achiam, who later took Brockman’s seat but wasn’t left with either of the pillows. (Achiam eventually did obtain one of the more standard black cushions.)

OpenAI did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

One longtime technology lawyer told WIRED that using cushions or pillows isn't exactly "customary," but noted, "it's not totally out of left field." Personally, he said, he has never seen lawyers use pillows or cushions during his trials, but then again, he's "never been involved in a trial that has lasted as many days as that one."

The core litigators in this case sit in comparatively luxurious leather chairs, though a couple do show signs of fraying, so maybe the padding isn’t as robust as it appears.

My last time in this courtroom for an hours-long stretch was in 2021, covering portions of the Epic Games v. Apple trial. But capacity was limited back then because of Covid concerns, so I had plenty of room to stretch out. This time around, the courtroom has been filled nearly to its maximum capacity—about 150 people—including bench seats for up to 90.

I thought about bringing my own cushion roughly an hour into my first day of the trial at the end of April, because, well, these benches are deeply uncomfortable. But I didn't want to come off as weak. None of the other two dozen or so reporters regularly in attendance—including one who is pregnant—seemed to bring cushions, at least, initially. So I went through a run of six days with my bottom and back getting sorer by the minute.

Last week, after a particularly brutal morning, I finally decided to bring in some help. I couldn’t find the well-padded seat cushion meant for stadium bleachers, so I settled for a “cooling” cushion passed out at the steaming-hot outdoor venues at the Tokyo Olympics. About two seconds into using it on Wednesday morning for the first time, I ruled it counterproductive. It was too small and too thin to offer any relief. My back got particularly stressed when furiously typing notes about the Musk-inspired jackass trophy, which reportedly once had its own pillow.

Four hours in, I gave up on the pillow entirely. But I noticed one New York Times reporter who eventually caved, as well as the courtroom artist—who has a particularly colorful cushion—remained seated on their pillows. Maybe I’ll find a better remedy for next week, when Gonzalez Rogers will hear arguments about potential penalties.

Maxwell Zeff contributed to this report.

Instagram’s New Instants App Is a Snapchat Clone for Thirst Traps

Wired May 13, 2026

Meta launched a new app on Wednesday, called Instants, that integrates with existing Instagram accounts and allows users to send unedited, disappearing photos. Instants leans into the popularity of Instagram’s Stories feature and Close Friends lists, where users can selectively share images with a smaller audience.

Instants is available as a stand-alone app on iOS and Android in select countries, and it’s accessible through Instagram’s direct messaging tab.

The core of Instants, from its name to the bare-bones layout, is designed to evoke a sense of ephemerality. Yes, it's a conceptual clone of Snapchat, with images that disappear after viewing, which can also be unsent before the person on the other end views them. (Instagram’s Stories feature, launched a decade ago, was also influenced by Snapchat.)

Unlike Snapchat, Instants is much more focused on capturing raw moments, like the once-viral BeReal app, and doesn’t allow any filters or retouching. That's striking for a company that helped make sepia-toned filters like Valencia household names, and is hell-bent on adding generative AI to every other corner of its apps.

There’s one specific kind of raw image I fully believe adult users will be sharing with their Close Friends list through Instants: dick pics.

Instagram’s Close Friends feature, which arrived in 2018, earned a reputation as a way to share thirst traps. As a gay man living in San Francisco, I’m fully aware of what I’m going to see when someone adds me to their list and posts to Close Friends. No one’s posting full hog on main—that would be blocked by Meta—but there’s plenty of skin on display in those green bubbles.

Similar to Instagram, Instants is available to teenage users. Even so, content posted on either app may feel adult in nature. While Instagram’s community guidelines ban posting most kinds of nudity, with exceptions for sculptures and breastfeeding, in practice, the main feed on my Instagram is full of ass shots—nothing frontal. Images posted on Stories just to Close Friends lists, rather than being more publicly shared, often seem to avoid the stricter moderation rules. The Instants app is governed by the same guidelines as the main Instagram app.

“All the safety and privacy protections built into Instagram apply to Instants, whether you're on Instagram or on the Instants app. Our nudity policies apply across Stories, Close Friends, and Instants - we use the same tools to keep people safe on Instants, including technology to detect and remove violating content (i. e. nudity), and a way to report issues, with serious safety concerns flagged for urgent review,” says Devi Narasimhan, a Meta spokesperson.

Even though this isn’t a secure way to share your nudes, I expect Instants to be the next evolution of a Close Friends thirst trap. It’s easy to set your Instants only to be sent to those already on your Close Friends list, and you can unsend photos that someone hasn’t opened yet. In addition, screenshots of your shared snaps are blocked by default. (Though, in a world where many households have multiple cameras, it’s easy to snap a pic of a screen.)

When you open the Instants app, you’re immediately greeted by an image of your own face staring back at you on the screen. The sparse layout includes buttons to flip the camera, turn on the flash, and see the Instants you’ve sent. There’s no option for video, only still images. A level of discretion is also given to your friends who view these images; users aren’t notified when you peek at their images, and only the person sharing the Instant can see your replies and reaction emojis.

In a way, any app or feature that’s promoted as ephemeral messaging will lead to spicy pics shared between adults. Snapchat was seen the same way at its launch, with a 2012 Business Insider headline reading: “Let's Be Real: Snapchat Is Totally Used for Sexting.” When Twitter, in the pre-Musk era, shut down a feature where users could post ephemeral tweets that disappeared after a day, called Fleets, many terminally online users spent the last day celebrating the feature with unhinged, skin-baring posts.

Instants—joining a growing repository of Instagram apps like Edits and Threads—may not stick around as a stand-alone app, but there will always be a segment of users who want to send cheeky shots to their friends in ways that feel less permanent than texting the group chat—and while horniness is universal, from my experience, it's a lot of gay men.
